subject: Pathology
summary: Oesophageal adenocarcinoma is a cancer of the distal oesophagus that usually arises from Barrett oesophagus after chronic gastro‑oesophageal reflux. It is most common in white men and progresses through dysplasia to invasive disease.

sections.p: A malignant tumour of glandular (adenocarcinoma) cells arising in the distal third of the oesophagus, most often on a background of Barrett oesophagus.
b: Diagnosis requires endoscopic visualisation + biopsy showing malignant columnar epithelium with gland formation
Barrett oesophagus is defined by intestinal metaplasia (goblet cells) in the oesophageal squamous mucosa

t.b: Does the lesion contain malignant glandular cells? Positive confirms cancer; negative with suspicious appearance prompts repeat or deeper biopsies
Identifies adenocarcinoma morphology and excludes squamous carcinoma; HER2 testing guides therapy if positive

sections.p: Staging follows the AJCC TNM system, guiding prognosis and treatment choice.
b: T1‑T4: depth of invasion from mucosa to adjacent structures
N0‑N3: number of regional lymph nodes involved
M0‑M1: distant metastasis

t.b: If CT unavailable, use chest X‑ray and abdominal ultrasound as a limited alternative
Accurately assesses T depth and regional N nodes. Positive nodes upstage disease and may alter surgical planning

sections.p: Most cases arise from chronic gastro‑oesophageal reflux leading to Barrett metaplasia, with additional lifestyle and environmental contributors.
b: Chronic GERD → Barrett oesophagus (primary cause)
Obesity (especially central adiposity)
Tobacco smoking
Radiation exposure (head/neck, prior therapy)
Low intake of fruits/vegetables (protective factor when high)

sections.p: Early disease is often silent; later stages produce dysphagia and weight loss.
b: Progressive dysphagia first to solids, then liquids
Unexplained weight loss
Odynophagia or chest pain mimicking heartburn
Occasional vomiting of blood (advanced disease)

sections.p: A stepwise approach combines endoscopy, imaging, and pathology to confirm cancer and stage it.
b: Endoscopy with systematic biopsies of any visible lesion and of Barrett segment
Cross‑sectional imaging (CT) for nodal and metastatic assessment
EUS for detailed T/N staging when available

t.b: Screens for structural obstruction when endoscopy not immediately available; shows narrowing or irregularity but cannot confirm cancer
Detects metabolically active distant disease; positive scan upstages to M1 and changes management

sections.p: Complications arise from tumour growth and treatment.
b: Obstructive dysphagia leading to malnutrition
Fistula formation to trachea or bronchi (rare)
Bleeding causing anemia
Metastatic spread to liver, lungs, bone

sections.p: Curative intent combines surgery, chemotherapy, and radiotherapy; palliative care focuses on symptom control.
b: Neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy (cisplatin‑based or fluoropyrimidine‑based) to downstage tumour before surgery
Surgical resection (transthoracic or transhiatal oesophagectomy) for resectable disease
Targeted HER2 therapy (trastuzumab) if tumour overexpresses HER2
Palliative stenting or radiotherapy for unresectable obstruction

t.b: Consider best supportive care, nutritional support, and referral for possible radiotherapy

sections.p: Survivors need surveillance for recurrence and for new Barrett‑related lesions.
b: Endoscopic surveillance every 6–12 months for Barrett patients after treatment
Lifestyle modification: weight loss, smoking cessation, increase fruit/vegetable intake
Control reflux with proton‑pump inhibitors to reduce further metaplasia

sections.p: Other oesophageal cancers and benign conditions can mimic OAC.
b: Oesophageal squamous cell carcinoma (proximal, tobacco/alcohol risk)
Benign peptic stricture from GERD
Achalasia (dysphagia to both solids and liquids early)

sections.p: Certain tests may give false reassurance.
b: Normal barium swallow does not exclude early mucosal cancer
Negative biopsy from a single site may miss focal carcinoma – repeat or deeper biopsies needed
CT may underestimate nodal disease compared with EUS

whenToSeekHelp: Rapid, unintentional weight loss (>5 % in a month)

faq.q: Why is Barrett oesophagus a precursor?
faq.a: Chronic acid injury replaces squamous cells with intestinal‑type columnar cells that are genetically unstable and can progress to dysplasia and adenocarcinoma.

faq.q: Can OAC occur without Barrett oesophagus?
faq.a: Rarely; most cases arise from Barrett, but de novo adenocarcinoma can develop in the distal oesophagus.

faq.q: Is screening useful in low‑resource settings?
faq.a: Targeted endoscopic screening of high‑risk groups (male, obese, chronic GERD) is cost‑effective where endoscopy is available.

exam: Describe the stepwise progression from chronic GERD to oesophageal adenocarcinoma, including key histologic changes.
Explain how the AJCC TNM staging influences treatment choice for oesophageal adenocarcinoma.
List three modifiable risk factors and two protective factors for this cancer.
